r.t: WALTER WHITE
Introduction

Walter White was an unassuming chemistry teacher when he was diagnosed with cancer. In order to save money for his family, he began a life of crime, in which he got more and more involved, eventually becoming one of the most infamous and dangerous drug kingpins in the world: Heisenberg.
In this doc, I’ll go over his feats from the show Breaking Bad, looking at the thought processes and machinations he employed throughout.

Note that this doc aims to scale the character as high as possible, which means I’ll sometimes be interpreting the source material, but keep in mind that the validity of any feat can always be contended in a debate referring to the doc. I don’t consider docs to be the be-all end-all of debating so cases like these are not me trying to wank the character but simply me getting the most juice out of what I’m given. I’ll make sure to be clear through my wording when I’m talking about fully confirmed segments and when I’m basing myself on implications or interpretations.

Keep in mind that I don’t think every subcat needs a thorough explanation, especially fluid/crystallized intelligence and certain thinking subcats (for example I don’t think that there’s a need to mention that Walter had to come up with an idea every time I write down divergent thinking), but I will give an explanation every time the use of one of these categories is notable.

Throughout the doc, I highlighted a few of Walter’s plans. My criterion was to do this only with plans that had a clear execution process and that were at least somewhat major. Strategies are trickier as they usually involve multiple episodes and get intertwined with other feats, so I didn’t do the same for those.

I left a summary in the end which you can find in the tabs. This is because the doc exceeds 260k characters and I have a feeling not many people will be willing to go through it all. The summary includes short descriptions of Walter’s most notable feats for each episode, so that if you are interested in reading the details on said feat, you can go back to the mentioned episode’s analysis and read the related section. Walter finds out that he has lung cancer. Under-paid and under-achieving, he decides to take up the offer that his brother-in-law, Hank, who is a DEA agent, gave him for a ride-along during a raid on a meth lab.

It’s time to tackle what is possibly Walter’s biggest anti-feat.

Hank has hatched a scheme to catch Walter, that being to convince him that Jesse is about to burn his money and then follow Walter to said money so as to catch him red-handed and get evidence of his theories. Hank’s plan is very well put together and involves extremely impressive information gathering, but I won’t discuss that in too much detail here. What I want to focus on are the factors that allowed this plan to be formulated and to work.

Hank’s biggest asset was, by far, Jesse. Jesse was the one to get the idea to use Walter’s money against him, who was able to point Hank to Huell as someone who would know something about where Walter took his money.

Both Hank and especially Jesse have personal experience with Walter, and this allowed them to anticipate that Walter would be too stressed upon hearing that Jesse is about to burn his money to read the situation properly. Hank even outright says that Walter wouldn’t be able to discern anything out of place in the misdirection because of how anxious he would be about the money.

The money in question is the result of Walter’s entire Heisenberg endeavor. It’s both what he’s supposed to leave to his family after he’s dead and a token of his power, pride, and achievements as Heisenberg. In short, everything that drives him as a person has massive stakes in the fate of this money.

And all of that is only a portion of the emotions that Walter feels as the trap is being sprung. When Jesse calls Walter to tell him that he’s about to burn the money, providing him with a picture of a barrel, Walter feels incredible anger on top of the desperation. This is because of how much he feels he has done for Jesse, prompting a feeling of betrayal, especially after he’s been holding off from killing Jesse until the very last moment, despite Saul and Skyler’s advice.

So, while this is a pretty big failure in emotional management, it’s somewhat excusable given the context, and doesn’t remove the fact that Walter’s feats in this category can be fairly remarkable in other situations. All this means is that when facing against such an extreme prospect as losing everything he has worked and bled for the last years, he can break.
Obviously, as I hope this doc has already proven, Walter’s falling into this trap doesn’t at all reflect his judgmental capabilities under normal circumstances.

Common Misconceptions
Now that I’m finished with the feats, I’d like to tackle some notions commonly believed about Walter that paint him as less intelligent or more incompetent than he actually is.
Walter is just lucky.
This is arguably the most common and most damaging belief about Walter’s achievements.
I have seen quite a lot of people claiming that Walter’s success was always due to luck, rather than skill or intelligence.

Now, there are instances of Walter having some good luck, but he’s not inherently luckier than your average character. In fact, I’d argue that for any example of good luck on Walter’s part, you could give two examples of bad luck.
Here are a few examples:
Tuco’s sudden outrage at No Doze indirectly leading to his lair being raided and thus his kidnapping of Walter.
Walter’s mention of having a second cellphone to Skyler while anesthetized for his surgery.
Jesse, by complete chance, getting in a relationship with the older sister of the kid that the dealers working with Gus use for their business, leading to the conflict with Gus.
Skyler giving the drug money to cover Ted’s tax evasion.
Jesse making Gus suspicious during the execution of the hospital trap.
Hank deciding to use the master bathroom and finding Gale’s book.
Jesse having his meth lifted off him by Huell, leading to his realization of Walter’s lily of the valley scheme.
Hank happening to be following Jesse to Walter’s house, leading to their alliance.

These are only some examples, but they paint the picture. While Walter might’ve had some good luck from time to time, more often he has been quite unlucky, forcing him to adapt to unforeseen situations.
Aside from that, a character being lucky at times doesn’t invalidate all of their feats by default.
Walter is inferior to Gus and only beat him through luck.
This is a sister argument to the previous one, and there are a few things to talk about.

Walter’s operation was not a long-term one like Gus’s. His goal was to make enough money throughout the two years he had left to live. Gus had twenty years to build up a rock-solid operation paired with a public enterprise in Los Pollos Hermanos acting as a front, not to mention vital help from Madrigal.

This is a continuation of my previous point, but I think it’s unfair to say Walter’s victory over Gus is just luck. What’s lucky about it is simply Hector’s existence as an emotional weakness of Gus’s. Walter very likely wouldn’t have been able to kill Gus, but this is not because Gus was smarter. Gus had simply a lot more influence and material power than Walter, making the task of killing him almost impossible. On top of that, the opportunity to kill Gus isn’t served on a silver platter. Walter discovered this connection through Jesse’s intel, which was a deliberate part of his strategy. Even then, someone as smart as Saul thought the information to be useless, while Walter intuited its importance and was able to infer a whole hidden aspect of Gus’s personality from it. And still, this only provided a vague opportunity. Walter still had to persuade Hector, adapt his strategy, and misdirect Gus to achieve his goal. To make an example from another work

: A similar argument would be to say that Light’s victory over L was completely luck-based because of the mere existence of the Shinigami Eye power. If that ability wasn’t a thing, L’s secret identity would’ve made it nearly impossible for Light to kill him, just as Gus’s power and protection made it nearly impossible for Walter to kill him. Both L and Gus had inherent qualities that made them hard targets for Light and Walter, respectively, and only the existence of a way to bypass said qualities (Shinigami Eyes and Hector) made them possible to defeat. Sure, there’s a degree of luck working in Light and Walter’s favor here, providing them with opportunities, but it’s minor compared to the initial bad odds they had, and even then, it took a lot of cunning and effort for each to capitalize on said opportunities. In all honesty, I’d even consider Light’s luck to be greater than Walter’s when comparing the two situations, but that’s beyond the scope of this example.

Besides that specific situation, I find the notion of Gus being smarter than Walter to be generally untrue. Gus is superior to Walter in some regards, no doubt, but in terms of sheer intellect, Walter is a man who was able to see right through Gus’s strategies basically every time. From Gus’s one minute strategy (the Twins vs. Hank), to his use of Gale as a substitute, to his manipulation of Jesse.
Walter is only capable of manipulating junkies.
Yes, I’ve heard this argument. Let’s get it out of the way.

Walter does indeed manipulate a junkie. Walter’s manipulation of Jesse is very advanced and shows how capable and shrewd he is. Just because Jesse is a “junkie” doesn’t mean he can be played with a few words. The methods Walter uses are clearly very thought-out and deserve analysis and consideration, and even then, they don’t always work. Is this because Walter is a poor manipulator? Far from it. Jesse, while not the brightest, has his moments of brilliance, some of which are even mentioned in this doc, though not in detail. Walter is not just using minor persuasion, either. More often than not, he’s actively pushing Jesse to go against his deep-rooted beliefs and morals, and for a big chunk of the show, Jesse was also being counter-manipulated by someone as cunning as Gus. All this is to say, manipulating Jesse is not as meaningless a feat as some make it out to be.
Besides that, the notion is also untrue. Walter, during the show, has successfully manipulated Skyler, Hank, Gus, Jack, Lydia, and more. So no, I’d say he can manipulate more than just junkies.
Walter couldn’t even keep his family from discovering his secret.

Technically true, but as I’ve already discussed at length, a lot of bad luck went into this. I also think it would be a disservice to Skyler to say that deceiving her is easy. She has solid reasoning, and she understands manipulative tactics enough to use them herself at times. Yet Walter was able to hide his secrets from her until he was literally sedated. Hank finding out is much more of a mistake on Walter’s part, but it’s still unlucky, and Walter would’ve been able to control the damage if not for Jesse. Something to mention about Hank, though, is that he’s a full-on detective with some very solid feats, like uncovering Gus’s operation, and someone who I could even consider low-tier SCD material.
Walter is sloppy and makes a lot of mistakes.
